title: Fostering learners’ self-regulation and collaboration skills and strategies for mobile language learning beyond the classroom
venue: Routledge Handbook of Language Teaching and Learning beyond the classroom
extended_summary:
This book chapter examines how self-regulated learning (SRL) and collaborative learning can be supported in mobile-assisted language learning (MALL) beyond the classroom. The authors argue that language learners need support to manage their own learning processes, collaborate effectively, and make productive use of mobile technologies across settings, especially as learning increasingly happens outside traditional classrooms.

Rather than reporting a single intervention study, the chapter reviews a sample of 20 empirical studies published between 2010 and 2020 on mobile language learning, SRL, and collaboration. The paper highlights mechanisms used in prior work, such as goal-setting support, dashboards, self-monitoring tools, peer feedback structures, and teacher-orchestrated collaborative tasks. It also discusses how learning analytics and artificial intelligence could be used to provide adaptive language learning paths.

The population context spans second/foreign language learners, including older K-12 students, university students, and migrant adult learners, though the chapter is especially attentive to out-of-class mobile learning contexts. The main conclusion is that mobile technologies can help foster SRL and collaboration, but effective design requires clear theoretical grounding, attention to learner support, privacy, and adaptive feedback. The chapter does not evaluate generative AI tools or reading/literacy outcomes directly; instead, it offers a conceptual and design-oriented synthesis for future MALL development.

identified_tools.name: Mobile Learning Apps (General)
identified_tools.description: Mobile-assisted language learning applications and related mobile learning systems used to support language learning outside the classroom, sometimes with adaptive or self-regulation features.
identified_tools.use_case: The chapter reviews empirical studies of mobile-assisted language learning and discusses how mobile apps and related designs can support self-regulation and collaboration in language learning beyond the classroom; it does not evaluate one specific named AI product.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed MALL studies, the chapter reports generally positive associations between mobile technology use and self-regulated learning, and suggests these technologies can support individualized and adaptive language learning paths. However, the chapter is a narrative synthesis of selected studies (20 papers) rather than a direct causal evaluation of a single AI tool.
findings.measure: Narrative synthesis of self-regulated learning and collaborative language learning outcomes in mobile-assisted language learning studies

findings.finding_summary: The chapter states that m-learning enhanced learners' SRL and SRL enhanced m-learning in the reviewed literature (Palalas & Wark, 2020 cited within the chapter, n=38 reviewed studies). It also notes that SRL behavior was the most important factor in predicting linguistic outcomes in one cited study, but the chapter does not provide direct effect sizes for that result.
findings.measure: Association between mobile learning and self-regulated learning; linguistic outcomes in cited studies
findings.sample_size: 38 reviewed studies (as cited in the chapter)

findings.finding_summary: For collaborative mobile language learning, the chapter reports benefits such as increased opportunities for communication, target-language negotiation, peer feedback, and writing quality/quantity, but also emphasizes that gains are hard to attribute directly to collaboration because many interventions mixed individual and collaborative components.
findings.measure: Collaboration-related language learning outcomes (communication, peer feedback, writing, speaking/listening practice) in reviewed studies

quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative book chapter synthesizing prior studies rather than reporting a controlled evaluation of one AI tool. The evidence is therefore descriptive and secondary, with no direct effect sizes reported in the chapter text.
impact_tier_rationale: The chapter suggests potentially meaningful benefits of mobile and AI-supported language learning designs, but it does not provide quantified impacts on K-12 reading/literacy outcomes relative to business-as-usual or non-AI supports. The strongest claims are qualitative and refer to heterogeneous studies with mixed designs.
